articles.title: Atlanta Dream vs. Golden State Valkyries pick, prediction, odds: Best bets for the WNBA Finals
articles.summary: Our WNBA handicapper gives his take on which team will win the finals, as well as his favorite bets in the series.
articles.body:
The WNBA Finals tip off on Saturday at the Chase Center, as the second-seeded Golden State Valkyries host the No. 4 seed Atlanta Dream.

Both of these teams pride themselves on defense, generating points off turnovers, shooting a high volume of 3-pointers, protecting the rim and emphasizing rebounding. It is very analytically sound basketball and what we commonly see out of the Oklahoma City Thunder and Boston Celtics, so it's not surprising these teams have reached the finals.

Once we knew the teams, there were still two major unknowns for this series that have started to be figured out.

The first was the location of the games, but that has been worked out and the Atlanta Dream will play at State Farm Arena (where the Hawks play), but change the start time of the games to better accommodate the event. I was hoping the games in Atlanta would be moved to Georgia Tech's arena — which is close by and seats only 9,500 fans — as it would create an edge for the Valkyries (which I'm backing in this series). Part of the home-court advantage is the shooters knowing what the lighting looks and feels like and helps set rhythm and depth perception. If Atlanta role players were in a new environment, it would weaken the home-court advantage.

The second unknown is the health status of the Dream's star point guard Allisha Gray. Gray has been dealing with an injury to her ring finger on her left shooting hand. She missed the previous two games against the New York Liberty and then it was reported she had a "small procedure" shortly after. I thought Gray would be out for the series, but now we are seeing videos of her at practice shooting (and making three 3-pointers in a row).

Let's discuss a series, Game 1 and player prop bet to take now for the WNBA Finals.

WNBA Finals: Atlanta Dream (-105) at Golden State Valkyries (-115)

I'm going to lump these two bets into one writeup, because the angle between the series winner and Game 1 winner is highly correlated. I think the Valkyries have a few edges to lean on in this matchup.

Golden State made the finals after series against Jess Sheppard and A'ja Wilson as the opposing bigs, and they made those players play well below their standard. Wilson shot 41.1% for the series, and Sheppard was at 34.8%. That is down from 52.7% and 57.5%, respectively — a major drop in efficiency.

The Dream made the finals on the heels of Angel Reese being the best player on the team and producing a lot offensively. With the combination of Gray probably being less effective with the hand injury (if she plays), and the Valkyries being a dominant defense against opposing bigs, I think the offensive focal points for the Dream will struggle.

Golden State will also put Defensive Player of the Year runner-up Gabby Williams on Rhyne Howard, and size up against Jordin Canada. The Valkyries also have a coaching advantage, as head coach Natalie Nakase is probably the best head coach in the WNBA. She won Coach of the Year last season, and finished second this season. Nakase had eight days to prepare for this series, and that time gap likely creates a bigger edge in game planning. While Atlanta head coach Karl Smesko is very good himself, they operate on different tiers where this edge goes towards the Valkyries.

I am backing the Golden State home-court advantage, coaching advantage, health advantage and defensive advantage for both Game 1 and the series.

Best bets: Valkyries -2.5 in Game 1 and Valkyries -115 to win the series

Player prop: Veronica Burton WNBA Finals MVP (12-1)

The head of the snake for the Valkyries switches off between Veronica Burton and Williams. It has been Williams for the majority of this season and she has gotten the top honors for All-Star, DPOY and All-WNBA team voting. However, she is a new addition this season and it wasn't long ago that Burton was claiming all of those spots. They are a very solid 1-2 punch. The pricing for the WNBA Finals market lists Burton as the fifth-most likely candidate to win MVP, rightfully behind Williams — but she shouldn't also be behind three different Dream players.

This market seems to be overindexing Williams' performance in the playoffs thus far. Williams is averaging 22.7 point per game (up from 14.4 PPG in the regular season), while Burton is down to 9.5 PPG (after averaging 12.2 PPG in the regular season). The playoff sample size is so small (six games), and heavily matchup dependent, so this feels like an overreaction to have them priced so far apart.

Burton could lead the team in scoring, assist, 3-pointers and also be an engine defensively. Buy the dip for Burton to win WNBA Finals MVP.

articles.title: Los Lakers cierran la pretemporada con más sombras que luces
articles.standfirst: Batacazo por 106-126 ante los Nuggets de Jokic (17+6+8) y aumentan las dudas sobre la era Doncic (15+4+2)
articles.summary: Batacazo por 106-126 ante los Nuggets de Jokic (17+6+8) y empiezan a surgir dudas sobre la era Doncic (15+4+2)
articles.body: Los Angeles Lakers cerraron la pretemporada con una derrota ante los Denver Nuggets (106-121) que dejó más dudas que certezas. El equipo de JJ Redick terminó con dos victorias y tres derrotas y evidenció que todavía necesita ajustar muchas piezas. Sin LeBron James, el reto es construir un proyecto competitivo alrededor de Luka Doncic, pero las primeras señales invitan a la cautela. El comienzo del partido fue especialmente preocupante. Denver se impuso por 36-22 en el primer cuarto y llegó a disfrutar de 17 puntos de ventaja, aprovechando los errores y la fragilidad defensiva de los angelinos. Los Lakers acabaron con un 42,7% de acierto en tiros de campo y 14 pérdidas de balón. La reacción posterior no bastó para esconder sus problemas ante una defensa intensa. Otra de las sombras está en la protección del aro y la capacidad para competir físicamente. Los Nuggets encontraron demasiadas facilidades cerca de la canasta -Nikola Jokic acabó con 17 puntos, 6 rebotes y 8 asistencias- y castigaron las dificultades de los Lakers para cerrar espacios y controlar el rebote. Walker Kessler, llamado a aportar presencia interior, terminó con seis puntos y seis rebotes. Si no mejoran en defensa, sufrirán ante los rivales más poderosos del Oeste. La salida de LeBron también obliga a Doncic a asumir una responsabilidad todavía mayor. El esloveno terminó con 15 puntos, cuatro rebotes y dos asistencias en 18 minutos, aunque perdió cinco balones. Austin Reaves aportó 19 puntos, pero la conexión entre ambos y el nuevo pívot aún necesita rodaje. JJ Redick tampoco tiene completamente definida su rotación. El entrenador continúa buscando la combinación más equilibrada para acompañar a Doncic y Reaves, mientras las lesiones y las pruebas de pretemporada dificultan la continuidad. "Busco equilibrio en las alineaciones y jugadores que se complementen y encajen entre sí", explicó Redick, según Los Angeles Times. La falta de claridad en los roles y la necesidad de más alternativas para organizar el ataque son cuestiones pendientes. Hubo algunos destellos, con aportaciones interesantes de Quentin Grimes, Sandro Mamukelashvili y Ziaire Williams, pero no suficientes para cambiar el balance general. Los Lakers necesitan reducir las pérdidas, elevar su intensidad defensiva y encontrar una identidad colectiva que vaya más allá del talento de Doncic. La pretemporada no dicta sentencia, pero el equipo angelino llega al inicio oficial con más incógnitas que certezas y la sensación de que la transición tras la marcha de LeBron será más complicada de lo esperado.

articles.title: NBA’s improved Eastern Conference makes Knicks and Nets’ goals more difficult in 2026-27
articles.summary: The defending-champion Knicks and playoff-hopeful Nets are competing for different things. But they do have this in common: Their respective goals will be mo...
articles.body:
The defending-champion Knicks and playoff-hopeful Nets are competing for different things.

But they do have this in common: Their respective goals will be more difficult to accomplish due to a transformed Eastern Conference that should have more contenders and fewer punching bags this season.

"You see what goes on. A lot of teams got better, and it's good," Knicks forward Mikal Bridges said. "Excited for all of the other teams; you love when the competition's high. Who doesn't love that?"

The Knicks remain, at the very least, the co-favorite to win the East after they steamrolled through the conference last postseason en route to their first NBA championship in 53 years.

Outside of the departure of valuable backup Mitchell Robinson , the Knicks bring back virtually the same roster, including their entire starting lineup.

But while the Knicks dominated a weakened East last spring, they should expect more top-end resistance this season.

The star-hunting Philadelphia 76ers added LeBron James and Jaylen Brown to a core already headlined by Joel Embiid, Tyrese Maxey and VJ Edgecombe.

Whether the new-look Sixers can build chemistry and stay healthy will likely determine their ceiling, but there's championship upside if everything clicks.

"I didn't leave my family [in Los Angeles]," James said, "to lose in the second round."

The Miami Heat acquired two-time NBA MVP Giannis Antetokounmpo in a franchise-altering trade with the Milwaukee Bucks , pairing him with fellow All-Star big man Bam Adebayo to form what should be the NBA's best defensive frontcourt.

The Heat lack depth and playmaking, which means there's a range of outcomes for how their season will go. But betting against a motivated Antetokounmpo probably isn't smart business — nor is discounting the possibility of Pat Riley adding another difference-maker before season's end.

The Detroit Pistons, who won 60 games last season, remain in the mix now that they've finally re-signed All-Star center Jalen Duren after a tense restricted free agency. So do the Boston Celtics, whose data-driven approach and a full season of a healthy Jayson Tatum should allow them to again compete for a high seed, even after trading Brown away.

The Cleveland Cavaliers are always an excellent regular-season team, and they just went to the Eastern Conference Finals.

After finishing as the No. 5 seed, the Toronto Raptors added Kawhi Leonard to a promising young core, while the Indiana Pacers — just one season removed from an NBA Finals berth — should be vastly improved with a healthy Tyrese Haliburton back from a torn Achilles.

So while the Knicks are surefire contenders, the same can be said to varying degrees about the Sixers, Pistons, Heat, Celtics, Cavs, Pacers and Raptors, too.

That's eight teams for six automatic playoff spots right there.

The Knicks will be focused on the top of the bracket as they try to become the NBA's first repeat champions since the 2017-18 Golden State Warriors.

On the other side of the Brooklyn Bridge, the Nets should set their sights on landing a top-10 seed and making the play-in tournament after three consecutive playoff-less seasons.

After tanking the past two years — without a top-five pick to show for it — the Nets are done prioritizing draft capital.

They added multiple veterans, headlined by Julius Randle, to elevate a group featuring Michael Porter Jr. and numerous first- and second-year players, including rookie point guard Mikel Brown Jr., the No. 6 pick in June's draft.

The Nets have a long way to go after winning only 20 games last season, but the Porter-Randle duo should at least set a floor. Breakouts by Brown or a second-year player such as Egor Dëmin would raise the ceiling.

The problem is that cracking the top-10 in the East won't be easy.

In addition to the eight teams mentioned earlier, there are the ascendant Atlanta Hawks, who will be more seasoned after testing the Knicks during last postseason's first-round series.

There are the Orlando Magic, who have made the playoffs three years in a row.

There are the Washington Wizards, who since January have added Trae Young, Anthony Davis and No. 1 overall pick AJ Dybansta in a major talent infusion.

And there are the Charlotte Hornets, who went 44-38 last season but have since traded away go-to LaMelo Ball.

To make the play-in field, the Nets will have to finish better than at least two of the 12 teams mentioned above. That's definitely doable — especially if injuries come into play — but far from a certainty during a season when fewer teams seem poised to tank.

The Nets will have to prove they belong in the play-in mix rather than at the bottom of the standings, where the rebuilding Chicago Bulls and Antetokounmpo-less Bucks might be the only teams with lower outside expectations.

"We're coming in trying to win," Randle said. "It's as simple as that. However we can help give the younger guys experience and confidence and help them fast track … to contribute to winning basketball, that's really all that matters. All I care about, at the end of the day, is winning, and I know that's what those guys care about."
authors: Peter Sblendorio, New York Daily News

articles.title: Timberwolves get major reality check despite LaMelo Ball, Anthony Edwards pairing from former head coach
articles.summary: The Minnesota Timberwolves enter the 2026-27 NBA season with one of the league’s most intriguing backcourts following the acquisition of LaMelo Ball to pair...
articles.body:
The Minnesota Timberwolves enter the 2026-27 NBA season with one of the league's most intriguing backcourts following the acquisition of LaMelo Ball to pair with Anthony Edwards. However, former NBA head coach Tyrone Corbin believes Minnesota's championship aspirations will ultimately depend on its defense rather than its offensive firepower.

Speaking with Kyle Odegard of NEXTPredict, Corbin expressed confidence in Ball and Edwards developing chemistry but questioned whether the Timberwolves can consistently slow opposing teams.

"They're going to have to get some stops at some point. Offensively, you look at the talent they'll have on the floor in those two guys alone, they're going to be able to score the ball. Do they have enough to figure out how to slow other teams?" Corbin said.

Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)

"There are some nights you just can't force your will on a team, and defense will save you. With Rudy Gobert anchoring in there I hope it will help some, but they're going to need to stay in front of their guys at some point."

Minnesota finished its preseason with a 3-3 record, including a 133-116 loss to the Chicago Bulls on Friday night.

Despite his defensive concerns, Corbin expects Ball and Edwards to complement each other offensively.

"Easy. They both are dynamic offensive talents. LaMelo can score from anywhere but he can really pass the ball. You have to make sure the guys on the floor with him are looking, because he will throw it from anywhere and get it there."

Tyrone Corbin believes LaMelo Ball, Anthony Edwards can thrive together

Ball's arrival gives Edwards another established offensive creator capable of generating scoring opportunities for himself and his teammates.

Corbin also believes their personalities will help accelerate the adjustment.

"He is a great, great young man. I think his personality, and the things I hear about Ant's personality, is that they'll mesh pretty quickly, and that talent on the floor will come together."

However, Minnesota faces considerable competition in a Western Conference featuring the Oklahoma City Thunder and San Antonio Spurs .

With Gobert anchoring the interior defense, the Timberwolves have an established rim protector. Still, Corbin emphasized that Minnesota's perimeter defenders must provide sufficient resistance to maximize the team's potential.

"They're going to be good, man. To have Edwards there, and then add a kid like LaMelo, and Rudy in the middle. With the way they're going to be able to score, if they can get some stops, they're going to be something to reckon with in the West."

The Timberwolves will begin their regular season Wednesday, Oct. 21, against Giannis Antetokounmpo and the Miami Heat on the road. The matchup tips off at 7:30 p.m. ET on ESPN, providing Minnesota an early opportunity to demonstrate how its revamped backcourt performs against Eastern Conference competition.
